title: Canberra Announced National Data Centre Rules in July and Never Wrote a Number Into Them. Victoria Has Just Written One, and It Is 150 Metres.

KEY FINDING
          Published 22 September 2026 at 05:52. Evidence-based. Source-cited. No sponsored content.

Estimated reading time: 7 minutes

In short. Victoria has banned new data centres from residential zones, imposed a 150-metre buffer between any new data centre building and the nearest home, barred siting near schools and childcare centres in rural areas, required new facilities to bring their own renewable generation and storage, banned drinking water for cooling, and made developers pay for their own grid connection and network upgrades. The Australian government announced a national framework with most of the same headings in July and has not yet produced an enforceable instrument. Victoria has produced numbers, exemptions and a named plan. The rules are not retrospective, eight applications already before the minister are untouched, and no commencement date has been set, so the enforcement is still ahead of the announcement. It remains the most specific data centre siting rule any Australian jurisdiction has published.

Victorian premier Ben Carroll released a Sustainable Data Centre Action Plan on 22 September 2026 under a heading that did most of the work by itself: "We Need Data Centres But We Set The Rules." [1]

The content is more interesting than the headline. New data centres will be banned from residential zones. A 150-metre buffer will be required between any new data centre building and a home. Siting near schools and childcare centres will be prohibited. New facilities must supply their own renewable generation and storage, matching new demand with new generation, and must cover their connection costs and any network upgrades they trigger. They must use recycled or other non-drinking water for cooling, and where that cannot be achieved immediately they must offset drinking water consumption and pay for the infrastructure upgrades required. They must produce traffic management plans covering construction and operation, and deliver a Local Investment Guarantee providing local benefits such as jobs, training places and parks, subject to consultation. [1] [2]

Carroll put it as follows: "In Victoria, we set the rules - data centres must power themselves, protect homes and pay their way." Planning minister Sonya Kilkenny was blunter about the mechanism: "Data centres must bring their own supply to protect our energy costs - and they can't be built near homes." Anthony Carbines, the minister covering AI and the digital economy, supplied the reassurance: "Companies like Amazon and Microsoft choose to invest in Victoria - that will continue within sensible guardrails." [1]

On 15 July 2026 the Australian government announced mandatory national standards for large data centres covering energy, water and location, including a requirement that facilities put at least as much energy into the grid as they take out, underwrite new power supply, pay their full share of grid connection costs, and minimise water use and pay for any additional water infrastructure they need. This site covered it at the time and took the announcement seriously: a government that had declined to legislate a dedicated AI Act was regulating the electricity and the water the machines run on instead, and the concrete layer looked like the harder of the two to evade.

Two months on, the federal framework is still a set of commitments. Victoria has produced the thing planning officers use, which is a number.

150 metres is the first enforceable quantity in Australian data centre siting policy. A commitment that facilities must "protect homes" cannot be applied at a planning counter. A minimum separation distance between a data centre building and a dwelling can be, and can be litigated.

The distinction is not a criticism of Canberra so much as a description of Australian constitutional plumbing. Planning is a state responsibility. The Commonwealth can set standards, condition funding and legislate on corporations and trade, but the instrument that stops a building going up at a given address is a state planning scheme. A national framework on siting always has to land in eight of these documents before it means anything.

Three gaps are worth stating plainly, because the announcement does not dwell on them.

The rules are not retrospective. They do not apply to applications already approved, nor to the eight currently before the minister. [2] In a market where the pipeline is the entire story, an exemption for everything already in the queue is a significant carve-out.

There is no commencement date. Carroll said the planning scheme changes would be made "as soon as possible" and declined to name a day. [2] Detailed location, siting, design and built-form guidance is to be developed through 2027. [3]

And the renewable requirement is a matching obligation rather than a supply obligation. "Match their electricity demand with new renewable generation and storage" is an accounting relationship between contracted generation and consumption. It is a real constraint, considerably harder than buying certificates, and it is not the same as a facility running on the power it built.

Belinda Dennett, chief executive of Data Centres Australia, called the changes disappointing and argued that the 150-metre setback "singles data centres out for a restriction that comparable industrial uses ... do not face." [2]

That is a serious point and it deserves a serious answer rather than dismissal. Warehouses, cold stores and light manufacturing sit closer to housing than 150 metres across Melbourne. What distinguishes a large data centre is not any single impact but the combination: continuous low-frequency noise from cooling plant that runs at full load on the hottest nights, a grid connection that competes with residential supply in the same constrained network, and water demand in a state that has lived through drought within living memory. Whether that combination justifies a distinct setback is exactly the question a planning scheme amendment exists to argue. It is not obviously wrong in either direction.

The Greens spokesperson Sarah Mansfield called the plan a "huge win" while demanding compensation for existing residents near approved sites and the publication of acoustic modelling and health advice. [2] Both criticisms point at the same hole: the rules govern what gets built next, and nothing in them helps anyone already living beside what got built last.

Victoria has 50 operating data centres. Australia has 162, holding about 1.5 gigawatts of capacity as of March 2026, and Victorian data centre energy consumption is expected to quadruple by 2030. [2]

There is a pattern forming across jurisdictions that argue about data centre siting, and Victoria fits it exactly. This site has recorded a local veto in Pennsylvania and a moratorium proposal in Ireland, and the same shape recurs: national governments write frameworks about capacity and investment, sub-national governments write the rules that determine whether a specific building goes up at a specific address.

For anyone planning capacity in a market with a federal structure, the practical consequence is that the binding constraint is rarely in the national announcement. It is in a planning scheme amendment published by a state or a county, with a number in it, and usually after the national announcement has already been reported as settled.

Australia now has both documents on the table. Only one of them tells a developer where they may build.

A CAUSE WORTH BACKING

Redesmere Is Spreading a Smile

Redesmere, a government supplier we rate for saving the taxpayer hundreds of millions, is raising money for Spread a Smile, the charity that brings joy to seriously ill children in NHS hospitals and hospices. We're glad to give it a boost.

The Alternative

EUROPEAN SILICON LANDS

Europe Ships Its First Server Processor Into a Machine Nvidia Still Powers

SiPearl delivered the first Rhea1 CPUs to Bull on 22 September for integration into JUPITER, the first European-designed processor in a European-built exascale platform. The Cluster has room for 162 Rhea1 nodes. The Booster that makes the exaflop runs 5,884 nodes of Nvidia silicon.

DELHI PICKS THE SITE

India Tells Microsoft to Build Beside the Power Stations

The IT secretary asked Microsoft to put its next data centres near generation rather than at the Chennai cable landing hubs, and offered faster approvals for it. Move the buildings inland and their gravity becomes domestic. Spain used electricity to restrain. India is using it to steer.

KIEL SWITCHES THE FLOOR

Two Hundred German Government Desks Now Run Linux

Schleswig-Holstein moved its state chancellery off Windows, the layer under the LibreOffice and Open-Xchange migrations it finished first. About twenty machines stayed behind, pinned by departmental software, and that residue is the honest measure of a public-sector migration.

PODGORICA WRITES IT DOWN

Montenegro Gives Itself Four Per Cent Global Turnover Fines

A 106-article statute follows the GDPR closely, reaches any firm that sells to or tracks people in Montenegro, and demands a named local representative. The clauses that let data leave the country stay dormant until EU accession, a date Podgorica does not control.

TWO BLUEPRINTS, ONE EUROPE

Europe Commissions Rival Designs for Its Own Eyes in Space

ESA handed parallel architecture contracts to ICEYE of Finland and Leonardo of Italy to design the EU Earth Observation Governmental Service, twelve months each with an eight-month extension. Buying two designs is unusual discipline. The budget that would build either one is still being argued over.

NINETEEN SIGNED, ELEVEN PAY

Europe Starts Funding Its Own AI Stack, Sovereign Models Included

The first AI project of common European interest covers the whole stack, from data processing to sovereign foundation models and an open AI platform, coordinated by Germany. Nineteen member states designed it. Eleven will grant the aid, and the silicon question is still open.

OTTAWA AND BERLIN BUY RACKS

Two Governments Funded an Alternative to the American AI Labs

Canada and Germany have committed up to 300 million Canadian dollars to Yoshua Bengio's non-profit safety lab, and it buys dedicated sovereign compute built in Canada by Hypertec and 5C. Germany gets a Berlin office and calls it technological sovereignty.

MADRID COUNTS THE LOCK-IN

Two Per Cent of Spanish Firms Have Ever Changed Cloud Provider

Two per cent of business customers have ever moved their main cloud provider and five per cent run more than one, while Amazon and Microsoft take 60 to 70 per cent of some segments. The regulator also warns that sovereignty and certification rules cost small European providers the most.

BRASILIA SETS TWO PRICES

Brazil Wants the Source Code for the Cloud It Owns

Redata suspends import duty, IPI and PIS/Cofins on data centre equipment for five years and asks for a tenth of the capacity back. The Nuvem Brasileira methodology asks who holds the keys, which jurisdictions apply, and whether the platform still runs after the partner walks away.

MADRID FINDS THE LEVER

Spain Wires Digital Sovereignty Into the Electricity Grid

A draft royal decree makes any data centre over one megawatt file a sovereignty declaration before the grid operator may sign its connection contract. Public sector workloads cannot leave the EU, telemetry and backups included. Serious unremedied failure can cost the connection permit.

TOKYO FOLLOWS THE POWER

Japan Drew the Map of Where Its AI Can Live

METI has certified eighteen GX Strategic Areas, nine of them for data centre clusters, and the entry test is a grid connection that can grow to a gigawatt. Land use deregulation and subsidy follow. Nothing in it says who gets to own the racks.

OTTAWA NAMES THE PROBLEM

Canada Wrote Five Rules Against Depending on American Data Centres

The framework opens by admitting Canada relies significantly on infrastructure outside the country for compute, cloud and storage. Twenty-three companies signed, including Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta and OpenAI. No enforcement, no timetable, no thresholds.

PARIS PICKS ITS SUPPLIERS

France Signed a Sovereignty Pact With Its Own Industry

Three years, two ministers, and a first workstream aimed squarely at collaborative office suites, AI intrusion testing and critical infrastructure security. The entry test bars any firm dependent on extraterritorial rules. The same document creates no privileged market access.

THE DEMAND-SIDE LEVER

Brussels Points 2.5 Trillion Euros a Year at Its Own Suppliers

The proposed Public Procurement Act writes a European preference into public buying for the first time, with power to exclude bidders from countries that offer no reciprocal access. It is also the enforcement surface the cloud sovereignty law has never had.

THE MONEY ARRIVES

Europe Finally Wrote a Cheque Big Enough to Matter

Mistral has raised 3 billion euros at a valuation above 21 billion, the largest equity round a European technology company has ever closed. It starts filling the supply-side hole in the EU's own sovereignty law. Samsung led the round.

THE PARALLEL WORKPLACE

Switzerland Is Not Leaving Microsoft 365

The Federal Chancellery's own paperwork gives its open-source workplace two stated purposes: digital sovereignty, and keeping the government running if Microsoft 365 is unavailable. 3,000 seats from the end of 2027, alongside the incumbent rather than instead of it.

EUROPE'S OWN INSTRUMENT

Europe Starts Logging Every Flaw Being Exploited Right Now

From 11 September the Cyber Resilience Act gives any manufacturer selling a connected product into the EU 24 hours to tell ENISA when one of its vulnerabilities is being exploited. Built by an EU agency, under EU law. The firms filing into it mostly are not European.

THE NEW DEFENCE

EU Antitrust Law Just Learned the Word Resilience

The Commission's first final Article 102 guidelines let a dominant company justify its conduct as supply-chain hardening. Twenty-eight economists warn the defence does not check the passport of the firm invoking it.

BRITAIN'S NEW LEVER

Ministers Move to Evict Risky Suppliers

New Cyber Security and Resilience Bill amendments would let the Secretary of State order a named vendor's technology removed from energy, water, health and data-centre infrastructure. Sovereignty as a standing administrative power, not a one-off ban.

THE EMPTY LADDER

The EU's Top Sovereignty Tier Has No Providers

Germany's 1,600 municipal utilities checked the market against CADA's four assurance levels: very few providers reach level 3, and level 4 has none at all. The pass mark below was audited. This ladder is still empty.

THE PASS MARK

A Public Cloud Just Passed France's Hardest Test

ANSSI has qualified OVHcloud's SNC Cloud Platform under SecNumCloud, the standard that requires immunity from non-European law. Italy, Germany and Poland are next. A sovereignty claim that was audited, not pledged.

THE OPPOSITE MODEL

Korea Gave the Training Data Away

Twenty-nine datasets, 35.44 million records and 11.3 terabytes from the national sovereign AI programme, free to any domestic company, researcher or student. Every other programme defines itself by what it keeps in.

A DATE, NOT A STRATEGY

Germany Has Given Itself Until March 2027

Sovereign alternatives available at official workstations across sixteen states by the end of March 2027. Bavaria walked away from a billion-euro Microsoft renewal and is piloting on forty desks. Schleswig-Holstein is already years ahead.

BRITAIN'S ATTEMPT

Sovereign AI Reaches the NHS Door

Lumen Sovereign, built from scratch on British public compute and designed to run air-gapped, now has a partner whose software sits behind NHS 111, GP practices and trusts. What it signed was a memorandum of understanding.

THE RULEBOOK

Portugal Wrote the Rule, Not the Press Release

Every public system classified by sovereignty, security and resilience, and the classification decides what a hyperscaler is allowed to touch. Backed by a law that makes you ask permission before you build.

EUROPEAN ALTERNATIVE

Sovereign Cloud Stack

German-led, EU-funded open project building a standardised, certifiable Kubernetes layer on European OpenStack clouds. The sovereignty fight above the virtual machine, where most migrations actually stall.

NEW ENTRANT

Office.eu Joins the Field

Euro-Office is no longer the only one. Office.eu, a 100% European-owned Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace alternative, launched in The Hague in March 2026: open-source core on Nextcloud, EU-hosted, in early access now.

THE REAL LOCK-IN

It Was Never About Word

The editor was the easy part. What kept the public sector on Microsoft was the compliance layer: legal hold, retention, classification. Nextcloud Hub 26 just shipped a self-hosted version of it, on data that never leaves your walls.

FRANCE'S ANSWER

France Pulls the Plug on Microsoft

Not a pilot, a mandate: every ministry ordered to plan its exit, La Suite NumÃ©rique already serving 500,000+ civil servants, and Teams and Zoom to be technically blocked on the state network.

STATE OF THE EXIT

Europe's Microsoft Exit, Mid-2026

From movement to migration: Schleswig-Holstein ~80% off Office, Denmark following, France ordering ministries to draw up exit plans, and Euro-Office shipped 9 June. The "no alternative" excuse is gone.
